analysis.one_liner: Imposes a two-year moratorium on major airline mergers and joint ventures while regulators study the effects on consumers.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred any large airline from acquiring or merging with another airline for two years, if the combined carrier would carry 10% or more of U.S. passengers. It would also have frozen merger-related changes to operating certificates, international route rights, and airport slots, and blocked large joint ventures and alliances among major carriers. In exchange, the Transportation Department would have studied how past airline consolidations affected fares, competition, service, and flights to rural communities, and reported to Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers, especially travelers in markets where mergers reduce the number of competing carriers, and residents of rural communities whose flight availability the bill specifically directed regulators to study. Smaller and new-entrant airlines also benefit, since the bill preserved slot access for new competitors and allowed small-carrier deals below the 10% threshold.

how_it_helps.text: It would block, for two years, any merger or acquisition that puts 10% or more of all U.S. passenger boardings under one carrier, slowing the consolidation of the industry into fewer, larger airlines.

It would freeze merger-related transfers of operating certificates, international route authority, and landing slots, so regulators could not hand a merging carrier the rights it needs to complete a takeover.

It would stop joint ventures and alliances tied to mergers from taking effect, including code-sharing and blocked-space arrangements affecting more than 15% of total available seat miles, keeping carriers from combining their networks in practice even without a formal merger.

It would require the Transportation Department to study and report to Congress on how past consolidations affected prices, competition, service levels, and the availability of flights in rural communities, creating a factual record before further mergers were allowed.

It contains exceptions for smaller carriers, for safety-related changes, and for slot changes that accommodate new-entrant airlines or small regional service, aiming to protect competition rather than just freeze the status quo.

analysis.who_pays: Major air carriers and their shareholders, who would lose the ability to merge, form alliances, or run joint ventures for two years. Airline employees and creditors of struggling carriers could also bear costs if a merger was a route to survival that the moratorium blocked.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major air carriers and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The moratorium was blunt: it barred all large-carrier combinations for two years, including mergers that might have rescued a failing carrier or its jobs, rather than judging each deal on its merits.

The definitions were broad — an ownership stake of just over 10% counts as 'control' — and the ban on joint ventures covering more than 15% of available seat miles could block cooperation agreements that benefit travelers through expanded networks.

Case-by-case antitrust review already existed as a check on airline mergers, raising the question of whether a blanket freeze was needed or would simply trade regulatory judgment for an arbitrary deadline.

The bill was introduced before the September 2001 downturn, after which the airline industry faced a severe financial crisis, and a two-year freeze on consolidation could have impeded restructuring at a time of distress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill rested on what consolidation does to travelers: fewer airlines on a route tends to mean higher fares and less service, and rural communities are usually the first to lose flights. A two-year pause with a mandated consumer-impact study gave Congress a chance to see the evidence before the next wave of deals. The case against is that the freeze was indiscriminate — it applied the same bar to a dominant-carrier takeover and to a rescue merger — and that antitrust review already screened individual deals. On balance, the bill traded some flexibility for a real check on a consolidation wave that passengers would pay for in fares.

outcome.mechanism: It was read once and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it simply expired when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on March 20, 2001, and spoke for it on the Senate floor, framing it as a response to the wave of airline consolidation then underway.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, its only committee referral.
The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

The bill was aimed at the merger wave of that period, in which American Airlines completed its acquisition of Trans World Airlines in April 2001 and United Airlines pursued a merger with US Airways until the Justice Department sued and the deal collapsed later that year.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major air carriers came out ahead: with no moratorium, they kept full freedom to merge, form alliances, and run joint ventures, and American Airlines' acquisition of TWA proceeded that spring. No protection was added for travelers or rural communities before the next round of consolidation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major airlines kept their freedom to consolidate

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Airline Merger Moratorium Act, spoke for it on the Senate floor, and referred it to committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: American Airlines and United Airlines
against.role: Major carriers driving the merger wave the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Pursued and completed acquisitions of other carriers during the period the moratorium would have covered.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party breakdown exists; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would block mergers, acquisitions, alliances, and large joint ventures among major carriers for two years. Consolidation among airlines reduces the number of competitors on individual routes, which tends to raise fares and cut service — a cost borne by travelers, not the carriers.

The bill exempts deals below the 10% enplanement threshold and protects slot access for new entrants and small-hub service, keeping runway for smaller competitors while the largest carriers are frozen.
By freezing merger-related transfers of landing slots, the bill keeps scarce slots from concentrating in merged carriers, while the new-entrant exception keeps some slots open for smaller carriers.
